title: Predictive Maintenance for Plastics Manufacturing: Where to Start!
summary: Unplanned downtime costs plastics plants more than the repair. Here’s a 5-step plan to start predictive maintenance, from first assets to proving ROI.
body_markdown:
## Key Points


- [Unplanned downtime](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/unplanned-downtime) hits plastics plants hard. Lines run continuously, material is scrapped when a machine stops and packaging customers expect on-time delivery.
- Industrial plants report a median downtime cost of $125,000 per hour, and research from ABB ranks plastics and rubber among the hardest-hit sectors ([ABB, 2023](https://new.abb.com/news/detail/107660/abb-survey-reveals-unplanned-downtime-costs-125-000-per-hour) ).
- [Predictive maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/predictive-maintenance) catches equipment problems weeks early, so repairs happen on your schedule instead of mid-run.
- You don't need to monitor everything to get started. Five steps get you there: know your downtime cost, pick your highest-risk assets, run a small pilot, build team habits and measure the results leadership cares about.
- For most plastics plants, the first assets to monitor are extruder gearboxes, injection molding hydraulics, chillers, air compressors and downstream packaging equipment.


## Why Plastics Plants Can't Wait for the Next Breakdown


Ask anyone who has worked a night shift in a plastics plant what a breakdown feels like. The extruder trips. Someone calls the maintenance lead late at night. And the scramble begins: find the problem, find the part, get the line back up before the shift's output is gone.


In plastics and packaging, that scramble costs more than the repair. Lines run continuously, so one stopped machine stops everything downstream. Material left in hot equipment starts to break down, so restarting means purging and scrapping it. And because packaging feeds directly into your customers' own production, a late shipment can stop their line too.


The pressure is only growing. U.S. manufacturing could need 3.8 million new workers by 2033, and 1.9 million of those jobs could go unfilled ([Manufacturing Institute, 2024](https://themanufacturinginstitute.org/manufacturers-need-as-many-as-3-8-million-new-employees-by-2033/) ). Fewer experienced technicians means less capacity to keep firefighting.


Predictive maintenance offers a better way.[Industrial sensors](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/sensors) watch your equipment around the clock, and AI flags problems while they're still small, often weeks before a failure. The repair becomes a planned job instead of an[emergency maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/emergency-maintenance) .


The hard part is knowing where to begin. These five steps will help you start small, prove the value and grow from there.


## Step 1: Know What Downtime Costs You


Before you choose any equipment, put a number on the problem. It shows you where to focus first, and it's the number leadership will want to see.


A simple way to estimate the cost of one failure:


**Cost of a failure = (hours down × lost margin per hour) + scrapped material + emergency labor + expedited parts**


For reference, industrial plants put the median cost of unplanned downtime at $125,000 per hour. At that rate, losing one eight-hour shift adds up to about $1 million ([ABB, 2023](https://new.abb.com/news/detail/107660/abb-survey-reveals-unplanned-downtime-costs-125-000-per-hour) ). Your number may be higher or lower, and it's often bigger than a downtime report shows. Scrap, overtime and rush freight rarely get tied back to the failure that caused them.


## Step 2: Pick Your First Assets


The most common mistake is trying to monitor everything at once. Start with the machines where one failure costs the most. Ask three questions about each asset:


1. **Is there a backup?** No redundancy means one failure can stop the line.
2. **What stops downstream when it fails?** The more output it takes with it, the higher it ranks.
3. **How long does a repair take?** Long lead times on parts turn hours into days.


In most plastics and packaging plants, these five asset groups rise to the top:


- **Extruder drives and gearboxes.** The extruder is the start of the line, and gearbox parts often have long lead times. One failure can mean days of lost output and scrapped material.
- **Injection molding hydraulics.** A wearing pump slows cycle times and produces inconsistent parts well before it fails. That means lower throughput and more scrap in the meantime.
- **Chillers and process cooling.** One central chiller often cools many machines. When it fails, it doesn't stop one press. It can stop every press it feeds.
- **Air compressors.** Compressed air runs controls, part handling and blow molding itself. Compressors run nearly nonstop and are easy to forget until they quit.
- **Downstream packaging equipment.** Winders, thermoformers, conveyors and palletizers turn finished product into shipments. When they fail, good product piles up and orders miss their trucks.


Use this as a starting point, then adjust it to your own floor.


## Step 3: Start With a Small Pilot


Begin with the machines that would hurt most if they failed: the ones that stop a line, create safety risks or cost the most to repair. Whether that’s five sensors or fifty, starting where downtime is most expensive shows value quickly and gives you real data to guide what to monitor next.


Before installing anything, clean up your asset records. Each machine should have accurate details like make, model, speed and bearing types. Better records lead to more precise diagnoses and fewer alerts your team has to second-guess.


Once sensors are installed, they monitor each asset around the clock, tracking vibration and temperature along with variables like ultrasound, RPM, runtime and energy consumption. Bringing these signals together gives your team one unified view of asset health instead of scattered readings. After a short learning period, the system knows what normal looks like for each machine and flags the changes that point to trouble early, like a gearbox bearing starting to wear or a hydraulic pump running hotter than usual.


## Step 4: Build the Habit


Sensors find problems. People prevent failures. A program only pays off when alerts turn into planned work, so set up a few simple habits early:


- **Name an owner for alerts.** Someone should check them every day and decide what happens next.
- **Hold a short weekly review.** Bring maintenance and production together to confirm alerts and schedule repairs around planned changeovers.
- **Turn alerts into**[work orders](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/work-order) **right away.** Nothing should get lost between the warning and the fix.
- **Close the loop.** After each repair, check the data to confirm the problem is actually solved.


Trust builds quickly once the team sees an alert lead to a real catch. That's when maintenance stops reacting and starts planning, and when[downtime](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/downtime) turns into scheduled time.


## Step 5: Measure What Leadership Cares About


Judge the program by the numbers your plant already reports. Record a baseline before the pilot starts, then compare after 90 days:


- **Unplanned downtime hours** on monitored lines
- [OEE](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/overall-equipment-effectiveness-oee) , especially availability
- [Scrap and purge losses](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/scrap-rate) from unexpected stops
- [On-time delivery](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/on-time-delivery) to customers
- [Maintenance cost](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/maintenance-costs) , including overtime and expedited parts
- [Planned vs. emergency work orders](https://tractian.com/en/blog/work-order-types)


Put a dollar value on every failure caught early using the cost formula from Step 1. A single avoided gearbox failure can make a strong case for the next wave of assets.


Then expand. Use what the pilot taught you to choose the next tier of assets, such as additional packaging equipment and support systems.

## Frequently Asked Questions


## What is predictive maintenance in plastics manufacturing?


Predictive maintenance uses sensors and AI to monitor the condition of equipment like extruders, injection molding machines and chillers in real time. Teams repair machines when the data shows a problem developing, not after a breakdown or on a fixed calendar.


### **Which equipment should a plastics plant monitor first?**


Start with assets that have no backup, stop the most production when they fail and take the longest to repair. For most plants, that means extruder drives and gearboxes, injection molding hydraulics, process chillers, air compressors and key downstream packaging equipment.


### **How is predictive maintenance different from preventive maintenance?**


[Preventive maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/preventive-maintenance) services equipment on a fixed schedule, whether it needs it or not. Predictive maintenance acts on each machine's actual condition. That helps you catch failures that develop between inspections and skip work on machines that are still healthy.


### **How do I build the business case?**


Start with your cost per hour of downtime, using the formula in Step 1. Multiply it by the unplanned downtime hours on your critical lines over the past year. That figure shows what's at stake, and the pilot shows how much of it you can recover.


### **How quickly will we see results?**


Many teams see their first early catches within the first few months, once the system has learned each machine's normal behavior. Larger drops in downtime and cost build as more alerts turn into planned work.


### **Does predictive maintenance replace our maintenance team?**


No. It gives your team better information, so they spend less time firefighting and more time on planned, high-value work. Technicians still confirm the problem and make the fix.
